final_writeup:
No full proof or counterexample is claimed: the target is precisely the Caccetta–Häggkvist conjecture, identified as open in the supplied text.

The rigorous progress is as follows. The conjectured bound holds for d=1 and d=2, for d>=n/2, whenever n<=2d+ceil((d+1)/2), for semicomplete digraphs, and for every digraph with n<=10. The supplied rainbow theorem yields both a universal constant-factor approximation and, for each fixed d, an additive-constant approximation.

A globally smallest counterexample would be an oriented, strongly connected, d-outregular graph with d>=3 and K=ceil(n/d)>=3. Every outneighborhood would contain a vertex of internal outdegree at most ceil(d/K)-1, forcing n>=3d+2-ceil(d/K). Thus a smallest counterexample with K=3 must lie in the narrow strip 3d+2-ceil(d/3)<=n<=3d.

The equality construction on Z_n, with arcs i→i+s for 1<=s<=d, has directed girth exactly ceil(n/d). Hence the requested bound, if true, cannot be improved in general.

results.claim: Tail-color reduction: if D has no antiparallel pair, form an undirected graph whose edge {v,w} has color v whenever v→w. Every rainbow cycle in this graph is a directed cycle of D of the same length.
results.proof_sketch: An undirected edge has a unique color because antiparallel arcs are absent. On a rainbow cycle C of length l, every edge color is one of its endpoints. Thus its l distinct colors are l distinct vertices of C, so every vertex of C is the tail of exactly one incident edge. The induced orientation of the cycle consequently gives every vertex outdegree one, which forces all edges to be oriented consistently around C.

Choose one outgoing arc from every vertex and iterate from any starting vertex. A vertex repeats within n+1 visited terms. The segment between the first repetition is a directed cycle of length at most n=ceil(n/d).

An antiparallel pair already gives the required 2-cycle. Otherwise retain two outgoing arcs per vertex and apply the tail-color reduction. There are n colors, each of size two. Theorem 1 in the supplied source, with p=0, gives a rainbow cycle of length at most ceil(n/2); the reduction makes it a directed cycle.

Without an antiparallel pair there is at most one arc per unordered vertex pair, hence at most n(n-1)/2 arcs. But minimum outdegree d gives at least nd>=n²/2 arcs, a contradiction. Thus there is a directed 2-cycle. Since d<=n-1, ceil(n/d)=2.

results.claim: Every such D has a directed cycle of length at most n-d+1.
results.proof_sketch: Let v1→...→vm be a longest simple directed path. Every outneighbor of vm lies on the path. If vj is the latest of its at least d outneighbors, then j>=d. The path segment vj→...→vm together with vm→vj is a cycle of length m-j+1<=n-d+1.

results.claim: There is a universal C<=10^11 such that every D has directed girth at most Cn/d.
results.proof_sketch: After excluding an antiparallel pair, retain d outgoing arcs per vertex and use the tail-color graph. The supplied source states the corresponding universal constant-factor rainbow-girth theorem. Its rainbow cycle becomes directed by the tail-color reduction.

results.claim: For each fixed d there is a constant alpha_d>0 such that every D has directed girth at most n/d+alpha_d.
results.proof_sketch: Apply the additive-constant rainbow-girth result quoted in the supplied source to the same n tail-color classes of size d, then invoke the tail-color reduction.

results.claim: If a counterexample exists, one of minimum order can be taken oriented, strongly connected, and exactly d-outregular; moreover d>=3 and K=ceil(n/d)>=3.
results.proof_sketch: A counterexample contains no antiparallel pair. Delete excess outgoing arcs at each vertex. A sink strongly connected component retains all d outgoing arcs; it is itself a counterexample because its order only decreases. Minimality therefore makes it spanning. The preceding exact cases exclude d<=2 and K=2.

results.claim: In a minimum-order counterexample, every outneighborhood S has minimum internal outdegree at most ceil(d/K)-1.
results.proof_sketch: Here |S|=d<n. Let r be its minimum internal outdegree. If r>=1, minimality says D[S] satisfies the target and hence contains a cycle of length at most ceil(d/r). Since the ambient counterexample has no cycle through length K, ceil(d/r)>K, so r<d/K. For integral r this is r<=ceil(d/K)-1. The assertion is immediate if r=0.

results.claim: Every minimum-order counterexample satisfies n>=3d+2-ceil(d/K). In particular, when K=3 it satisfies 3d+2-ceil(d/3)<=n<=3d.
results.proof_sketch: Choose v with indegree at least d and put S=N+(v). By the preceding claim choose u in S with at least d-ceil(d/K)+1 outgoing arcs outside S. None can be v, giving a 2-cycle, or an inneighbor of v, giving the triangle v→u→w→v. Thus {v}, S, N-(v), and these additional outneighbors are disjoint. Counting gives the inequality. The upper bound for K=3 follows from ceil(n/d)=3.

results.claim: If n<=2d+ceil((d+1)/2), then D has a directed cycle of length at most 3.
results.proof_sketch: Assume otherwise and trim to outdegree d. Choose v with indegree at least d and set S=N+(v). The oriented graph on S has at most d(d-1)/2 arcs, so some u in S has at most floor((d-1)/2) outneighbors in S. Its other ceil((d+1)/2) outneighbors are neither v nor in N-(v), since those alternatives create a 2- or 3-cycle. Hence n>=1+2d+ceil((d+1)/2), contradicting the displayed hypothesis. Combined with the d>=n/2 case, this proves the target throughout this parameter range.

results.claim: For d=3 and n<=9, D has a directed cycle of length at most 3.
results.proof_sketch: Assume not and trim to outdegree three. For arbitrary v, its three outneighbors induce an acyclic digraph, so choose an internal sink u. All three outneighbors of u avoid v, N+(v), and N-(v), or form a 2- or 3-cycle. Thus n>=1+3+3+d-(v). If n<=9, every vertex has indegree at most two, contradicting average indegree three.

results.claim: For d=3 and n=10, D has a directed cycle of length at most 4.
results.proof_sketch: Assume no cycle through length four. The preceding sink argument gives d-(v)<=3 for every v; averaging makes D 3-in/3-out regular. Fix v and partition the other vertices into S=N+(v), I=N-(v), and the three nonneighbors R. There are no arcs S→I. If every r in R receives an arc from S, then no r→I is possible, since v→s→r→i→v would be a 4-cycle; vertices of I could then receive at most two arcs, contradicting indegree three. Hence some r0 receives no arc from S. Since S sends nine arcs into S∪R and has at most three internal arcs, at least six go to R. The other two R-vertices can receive only six altogether, so S has exactly three internal arcs and is a transitive tournament. Its sink sends all three outgoing arcs to R, including r0, contradiction.

results.claim: The target holds for semicomplete digraphs.
results.proof_sketch: An antiparallel pair settles the claim. Otherwise D is a tournament. Minimum outdegree at least one prevents it from being transitive, so it has a directed cycle. A shortest tournament cycle has length three: for a cycle of length at least four, the chord between its first and third vertices creates either a triangle or a shorter cycle. Finally d is at most the tournament's average outdegree (n-1)/2, so ceil(n/d)>=3.

results.claim: The target holds for every n<=10.
results.proof_sketch: Use the d=1 and d=2 cases, and the 2-cycle argument when d>=n/2. The preceding two claims handle d=3. If d>=4, d<n/2, and n<=10, the only possibilities not already covered have d=4 and n=9 or 10; the three-cycle bound applies because both are at most 2d+ceil((d+1)/2)=11.

results.claim: For every 1<=d<n, the circulant digraph on Z_n with arcs i→i+s mod n for 1<=s<=d has directed girth exactly ceil(n/d).
results.proof_sketch: Along a directed cycle, lift every arc to an increment s in {1,...,d}. The positive increments sum to a positive multiple of n, so a cycle of length l satisfies ld>=n and l>=ceil(n/d). Conversely, for L=ceil(n/d), take L-1 increments equal to d and the last increment n-(L-1)d, which lies in {1,...,d}. Their proper partial sums are strictly between 0 and n, so they form a simple directed L-cycle. Thus even the natural stronger bound ceil(n/d)-1 is false.
